newsitem.title: USA: Court upholds California's affirmative action ban.
newsitem.headline: Court upholds California's affirmative action ban.

text.p: A federal appeals court on Tuesday upheld California's controversial Proposition 209, the first state law to bar 30 years of affirmative action programs.
The ruling by the three-judge panel was a blow to civil rights groups and the Clinton administration which had supported legal action to overturn the law.
California state Attorney General Dan Lungren said the ruling affirmed the "sovereignty of the people's right to create law at the ballot box."

Proposition 209, the first of its kind passed by any state, bars preferential treatment based on race or gender in public employment, education and contracting in California. The measure was approved in November by a margin of 54 percent to 46 percent after an intense period of debate in the state.
President Bill Clinton, asked about the court ruling in Washington, said: "We'll all have to regroup and find new ways to achieve the same objective."
He added: "My formulation of 'mend it, don't end it,' I still think is the best thing for America."
Soon after the proposition was passed in November, a federal judge blocked enforcement of the initiative, saying the measure probably violated the constitutional right to equal protection.
In its ruling Tuesday, the Appeals Court overturned the injunction, saying "we must conclude that, as a matter of law, Proposition 209 does not violate the United States Constitution."

"A system which permits one judge to block with the stroke of a pen what 4,736,180 state residents voted to enact as law tests the integrity of our constitutional democracy," the appeals court said in its ruling.
California Gov. Pete Wilson, a Republican who strongly backed the initiative, hailed the decision.
"Today we have seen justice served," Wilson told reporters.
The American Civil Liberties Union, which sued to block Proposition 209, said it would review its legal options and was likely to appeal.
"This ruling goes against the challenge to make sure that there's equal opportunity of women and minorities," said Elaine Elinson, an ACLU spokesperson.
The ACLU could appeal the decision to an expanded panel of the appeals court and to the U.S. Supreme Court.
Proposition 209 came two years after Californians approved another racially charged measure to cut off services to illegal immigrants. That initiative has been tied up in the courts ever since.
Affirmative action policies have been used in the United States since the 1960s to expand opportunities for women and racial minorities.

Supporters of Proposition 209 claimed racial and gender preferences were unfair and discriminated against people who might be better qualified. But opponents said minorities and women still faced discrimination in education and the workplace and affirmative action policies were needed to "level the playing field."
Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole and California's Wilson supported the measure while President Clinton, retired Gen. Colin Powell and civil rights leader Jesse Jackson opposed it.
